snapshot.title: UPSC Environment: NGT & CPCB Roles
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ UPSC v12.0 Hook: NGT: 2010. CPCB: Water Act 1974. Appeal: SC. Natural Justice: Core Principle.

quick_notes.title: NGT (National Green Tribunal)
quick_notes.detail: Est. 2010 under NGT Act. 3rd country in world (after Australia/NZ) to have such body. HQ : Delhi. Benches : Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai.
quick_notes.explanation: NGT (National Green Tribunal) is a special court set up in the year 2010 to handle cases related to environmental protection and conservation of forests and other natural resources. It was created by a law called the National Green Tribunal Act, which is why we say it was established under the NGT Act. India is the third country in the world to have such a dedicated environmental court, after Australia and New Zealand. The main office, called the headquarters or HQ, is located in New Delhi. The NGT also has four regional branches, called benches, which are set up in Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, and Chennai to hear cases from different parts of the country.

quick_notes.title: NGT Powers
quick_notes.detail: Not bound by Civil Procedure Code; guided by Principles of Natural Justice. Can award compensation. Appeals lie directly to Supreme Court.
quick_notes.explanation: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is a special court set up to handle cases about environmental issues. The NGT is not bound by the Civil Procedure Code, which is the usual set of rules for civil court cases; instead, it follows the Principles of Natural Justice, which are basic rules of fairness like giving both sides a chance to be heard. The NGT has the power to award compensation, meaning it can order a person or company to pay money for damage caused to the environment or to people's health. If someone disagrees with a decision made by the NGT, they can appeal directly to the Supreme Court of India, which is the highest court in the country.

quick_notes.title: CPCB (Central Pollution Control Board)
quick_notes.detail: Statutory body est. 1974 under Water Act. Powers under Air Act too. Advisory to Central Government and coordinates SPCBs.
quick_notes.explanation: CPCB stands for Central Pollution Control Board, which is a statutory body, meaning it was created by a specific law passed by Parliament, established in 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act. This law gave the CPCB the main job of preventing and controlling water pollution. Later, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act also gave the CPCB powers to handle air pollution. The CPCB acts as an advisor to the Central Government on pollution matters and coordinates the work of all the State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs), which are similar bodies at the state level. Its key functions include setting national standards for water and air quality, collecting and publishing data on pollution, and conducting research to improve pollution control methods.

quick_notes.title: SPCB (State PCB)
quick_notes.detail: Implement pollution laws at state level. Can shut down industries for non-compliance.
quick_notes.explanation: SPCB (State Pollution Control Board): A Complete Mini-Lesson for First-Time Learners SPCB stands for State Pollution Control Board, which is a government body set up in each Indian state to enforce pollution control laws within that state. Its main job is to implement laws like the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, by issuing permits, monitoring factories, and checking air and water quality. If a factory or industry breaks these laws by releasing harmful waste or smoke, the SPCB has the legal power to order that factory to shut down its operations immediately. It can also suspend or cancel the factory's consent or license, which means the business cannot run legally until it fixes the pollution problem. The SPCB works under the overall guidance of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) at the national level to ensure uniform standards across the country.

quick_notes.title: Bhopal Gas Leak Legacy
quick_notes.detail: Led to EPA 1986 (Umbrella Act). NGT is the specialized body to handle its technical disputes.
quick_notes.explanation: In 1984, a gas leak from a pesticide factory in Bhopal, India, killed thousands of people and caused long-term health and environmental damage. This disaster led to the creation of the Environment Protection Act (EPA) of 1986, which is an umbrella law that gives the central government broad powers to protect and improve the environment, covering air, water, land, and noise pollution. The EPA is called an umbrella act because it fills gaps left by older, specific laws like the Water Act and Air Act, and it allows the government to set standards and regulate hazardous industries. Later, to handle complex environmental disputes more efficiently, the government established the National Green Tribunal (NGT) in 2010. The NGT is a specialized court that only hears cases related to environmental protection, forest conservation, and issues arising from laws like the EPA, making it faster than regular courts. So, the Bhopal tragedy directly pushed India to create a strong general environmental law (EPA) and a dedicated court (NGT) to enforce it.
